purpose: Oxacillin is used to treat serious bacterial infections, especially those caused by a germ called Staphylococcus aureus (staph). It is commonly used for skin and soft tissue infections, bone infections, and infections of the heart or bloodstream. Your doctor has prescribed it because it works well against certain types of staph bacteria that other penicillins cannot fight.
how_it_works: Oxacillin works by attacking the outer wall that bacteria need to survive. Think of bacterial cells like a fortress with walls — oxacillin punches holes in that wall, causing the bacteria to fall apart and die. Your immune system can then clean up the rest of the infection more easily.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach upset. You may also notice redness or irritation at the injection site if given through an IV. Some people develop a mild skin rash. These effects are usually temporary and not dangerous.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you are allergic to penicillin or any other antibiotics, as this could cause a serious allergic reaction including difficulty breathing or swelling of the face. Oxacillin can sometimes affect your liver, so let your doctor know if you notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, or dark urine. Take the full course of treatment even if you feel better early, otherwise the infection may come back stronger.
typical_dosing: Oxacillin is usually given by injection or IV in a hospital setting because it is reserved for serious infections. Dosing typically ranges from 250 mg to 2 grams every 4 to 6 hours, depending on how serious your infection is and how much you weigh. Your healthcare team will set the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
